scenes.name: Joy Division
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: De Warsaw, rock pesado con influencias punk, a la desolación ballardiana: la originalidad crece a medida que las canciones se vuelven lentas y ralas, con el bajo de Peter Hook llevando la melodía, la guitarra de Bernard Sumner abriendo huecos, la batería de Stephen Morris rodeando un cráter y Ian Curtis recitando desde «un lugar solitario». Martin Hannett, productor de Factory, convierte el espacio en «control atmosférico» con delays digitales y grabaciones separadas: Unknown Pleasures (1979), con la portada del púlsar de Peter Saville, «Transmission», «Atmosphere». El coqueteo con la imaginería nazi, la epilepsia, los barbitúricos y un matrimonio roto desembocan en Closer, «estar dentro de la cabeza de Curtis», y en su suicidio en mayo de 1980. «Love Will Tear Us Apart» es su primer hit. Los supervivientes empiezan de cero como New Order.

scenes.name: New Order
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Los supervivientes de Joy Division, perdidos tras la muerte de Curtis («Ceremony», Movement), echan a Martin Hannett, aprenden a programar cajas de ritmos con música electrónica italiana y descubren en Nueva York los clubes chic, la emisora Kiss FM, los remixes de Pettibone, el freestyle y el electro. «Everything's Gone Green» (1981) marca el giro; «Blue Monday» (1983) y «Confusion», producido por Arthur Baker, los convierten en una banda de baile. Con Factory abren The Haçienda, inspirada en Danceteria y Funhouse.

xref.title: Pre-Suicide Activities (1980)
xref.body: In the days leading up to his death, Ian seemed to be in good spirits, with no seizures reported. On Thursday, May 15th, 1980, he played pool with bassist Peter Hook. The next day, Peter dropped Ian off at his parents' house with instructions to pack for the upcoming American tour. On Saturday, May 17th, Ian bailed on plans to water ski with guitarist Barney Sumner, citing a need to rest and wanting to watch a cool movie on TV. "On Thursday May 15th, 1980, Ian hung out with bass player Peter Hook playing pool in a local pub."

xref.title: The Haçienda Nightclub (1982–1997) – Millions Lost, Band Driven to Near-Bankruptcy
xref.body: In 1982, New Order were convinced to invest in building and running a nightclub in their Manchester hometown called the Haçienda. Having no knowledge of club management, they poured millions of pounds into the venture across 15 years, nearly bankrupting themselves. All their New Order and Joy Division album revenues were effectively swallowed by it. The club was culturally important as ground zero for the rave and dance culture explosion of the late 1980s, but was plagued by financial losses, security problems, and drug-related deaths (patrons preferring ecstasy over alcohol made the bar nearly unviable). It closed permanently in June 1997 and was converted to condominiums. Bassist Peter Hook wrote a book about the experience called *How Not to Run a Club*. "The profits of which were largely lost in the sinkhole that was the Haçienda nightclub."

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

xref.title: "Accident of Laziness" Origin of Dance Sound
xref.body: New Order's groundbreaking electronic sound and worldwide alt-rock influence partly originated from their reluctance to perform encores. They initially played Stephen Morris's drum machine alone as they left the stage, later adding a sequencer for Gillian Gilbert's synthesizers, and finally, Bernard Sumner conceived sequencing Peter Hook's bass line, leading to songs performed largely by machines. "But their worldwide success and the way they changed alt rock forever was due to an accident of laziness."

xref.title: Evolution of Bass Programming
xref.body: Peter Hook's later work in New Order involved programming bass lines and drum machines with drummer Stephen Morris. This collaborative approach significantly contributed to the band's unique sound, making it greater than the sum of its individual parts. "Later, his work in programming bass lines and drum machines with new order drummer Stephen Morris made that band into something much more than the sum of its parts."

xref.title: Evolution of Playing Style
xref.body: Over time, Flea abandoned his prominent slap-bass style in favor of a more melodic approach, characterized by fewer notes, more motion, and less frantic playing. This shift was influenced by bassists like Simon Gallup of The Cure and Peter Hook of Joy Division. "The slap-style has been all but abandoned in favor of a more melodic approach."

xref.title: Final Gig as Warsaw
xref.body: The band performed their last gig under the name Warsaw on New Year's Eve, 1977, before officially adopting "Joy Division." "So after one last gig as Warsaw on New Year's Eve 1977, Ian Curtis, Barney Albrecht, soon to become Bernie Sumner, Peter Hook and Steven Morris became Joy Division officially."

xref.title: Formation After Joy Division
xref.body: Following the death of Ian Curtis and the honoring of Joy Division's "suicide pact," Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word to dissolve Joy Division and immediately began working on their next project, which eventually became New Order. "So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word. Joy Division was retired, and work was started on the next project, which would eventually be known as New Order."

xref.title: Formation and Name Origin
xref.body: After Ian Curtis's death, surviving Joy Division members Bernard Sumner, Peter Hook, and Stephen Morris discussed their future. Encouraged by their progress as Joy Division, they decided to move forward under a new name. Their manager, Rob Gretton, suggested "New Order" after finding the phrase in a newspaper headline about mass killings in Pol Pot's Cambodia. "Their manager, my name Rob Greten, is the one who came up with it. He found the name in a newspaper headline about the mass killings in Pol Potts, Cambodia. The phrase was new order."

xref.title: Formation of the Band
xref.body: Ian's interest in music intensified after being one of a few dozen people to see the Sex Pistols play the Manchester Free Trade Hall on July 20, 1976, easily identifiable by his jacket with the word "hate" on the back. He then formed a band with Peter Hook and Bernard Albrecht, two guys he kept bumping into again and again at concerts, including that Pistols gig. "His interest in music really took off when he was one of a few dozen people in the audience, when the sex pistols played the Manchester Free Hall on July 20th, 1976."

xref.title: Makeshift Amplifier Solution
xref.body: Lacking money for an amplifier, Peter Hook and Barney ingeniously wired their instruments through the tone arm of a turntable in a family's console stereo, which provided enough sound for their early efforts. "He neither had any money for an amplifier so they figured out how to wire their gear through the tone arm of the turntable in a console stereo and buy one of their families."

xref.title: Peter Hook – Invented High-Register Bass Style Out of Necessity
xref.body: Peter Hook developed his distinctive style of playing bass high up the neck — in registers typically occupied by lead guitar — out of the practical need to be heard in Joy Division's dense sound. This approach became a defining characteristic of post-punk and new wave bass playing and proved highly influential. "His unique style arose from the need to be heard, playing the bass in the highest notes of the neck."

xref.title: Sequencing Bass Line Idea
xref.body: Bernard Sumner, the singer for New Order, originated the idea of sequencing a bass line from Peter Hook. This concept was pivotal in establishing the foundations of a new song played entirely by machines, influencing the band's future electronic direction. "It was singer Bernard Sumner who came up with the idea of sequencing a line in from bass player Peter Hook."

xref.title: Suicide Pact and Band Dissolution
xref.body: A solemn suicide pact existed among the members of Joy Division, stipulating that if any member were to leave the band for any reason, Joy Division would cease to exist. Consequently, upon Ian Curtis's death, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris honored their word, retiring Joy Division and beginning work on their next project, New Order. "The deal was that should any member leave for any reason joy division would be broken up. So once Ian was gone, Peter Hook, Barney Sumner, and Stephen Morris kept their word."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

xref.title: Unconventional Bass Technique Origin
xref.body: Peter Hook, inspired by punk's DIY ethos, initially played bass without formal training. His bass was slung too low, his stance was wrong, and his amp was underpowered. To be heard over loud drums and guitars during pub rehearsals, he started playing parts much higher on the fretboard, which inadvertently advanced the sound of rock and roll. "So to cut through the din, he started playing his parts far, far higher on the fretboard than normal."
